title: Chapter 4 — Of Slavery
paragraphs: THE natural liberty of man is to be free from any superior power on earth, and not to be under the will or legislative authority of any man, but to have only the law of nature as his rule. The liberty of man in society is to be under no legislative power except the one established by consent in the commonwealth, and under the dominion of no will and the restraint of no law except what that legislative enacts in accordance with the trust placed in it. Freedom, then, is not what Sir Robert Filmer tells us it is (Observations, A. 55): “a liberty for every one to do what he likes, to live as he pleases, and not to be tied by any laws.” The freedom of men under government is to have a fixed rule to live by, common to everyone in that society and made by the legislative power set up in it. It is a liberty to follow my own will in everything where that rule is silent, and not to be subject to the changeable, uncertain, unknown, arbitrary will of another man. In the same way, freedom of nature is to be under no restraint other than the law of nature.

This freedom from absolute, arbitrary power is so necessary to a man’s preservation, and so closely bound up with it, that he cannot give it up except by something that forfeits his preservation and his life together. For since a man does not have power over his own life, he cannot, by compact or by his own consent, make himself anyone’s slave, or put himself under another’s absolute, arbitrary power to take his life whenever that other pleases. Nobody can give more power than he has himself, and a man who cannot take his own life cannot give anyone else power over it. It is true that if a man has, through his own fault, forfeited his life by some act that deserves death, the person to whom he has forfeited it may, once he has him in his power, put off taking it and make use of him for his own service; and this does him no injury. For whenever the slave finds that the hardship of his slavery outweighs the value of his life, it is in his power to bring on himself the death he wants by resisting his master’s will.

This is the complete condition of slavery, which is nothing other than the state of war continued between a lawful conqueror and a captive. For if they once enter into a compact, agreeing on limited power on one side and obedience on the other, the state of war and slavery ends for as long as the compact lasts. As has already been said, no man can by agreement hand over to another what he does not have himself: a power over his own life.

I admit that we find, among the Jews as well as other nations, that men did sell themselves. But plainly this was only into hard service, not into slavery. It is clear that the person sold was not under an absolute, arbitrary, despotic power, because the master could not have had the power to kill, at any time, a man whom he was obliged to release from his service at a fixed time. The master of such a servant was so far from having arbitrary power over his life that he could not even maim him at will: the loss of an eye or a tooth set the servant free (Exod. xxi.).
